claims.text: Successful formation of homogeneous noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles is governed by temporal synchronization of precursor decomposition and metal-ion reduction across all components.
Tightly overlapping reduction kinetics with rapid nucleation curtails atomic diffusion.
Curtailing atomic diffusion arrests phase segregation and produces a uniform alloy structure.
The starting precursors are uniformly dispersed in a support or solvent matrix.
The precursor components have distinct but closely spaced decomposition or reduction temperatures.
A rapid thermal ramp and brief dwell at the nucleation temperature can synchronize reduction of all metal ions.
A controlled or inert atmosphere avoids oxidation during processing.
Thermal ramp and hold times are critical for concurrent nucleation of all elements.
A transient disordered, potentially amorphous cluster state forms at the nucleation temperature.
The transient cluster state enables rapid, homogeneous nucleation before significant diffusion causes elemental segregation.
Synchronized precursor reduction compresses the time available for atomic diffusion.
The compressed diffusion window kinetically traps the elements in a mixed state.
Kinetic trapping prevents large-scale elemental redistribution, phase separation, and segregation.
The rapid synchronized process will produce nanoparticles with a homogeneous alloy composition and uniform elemental distribution.
Conventional slower thermal processing with prolonged high-temperature exposure tends to cause phase separation, elemental segregation, or non-uniform morphology.
The proposed mechanism applies primarily when precursor decomposition temperatures and reduction kinetics are sufficiently close to permit synchronization.
The mechanism may not apply when precursor thermal properties differ too greatly.
The mechanism may not apply when solvents, stabilizers, or other extrinsic factors dominate reduction kinetics.
A synchronized thermal profile should significantly improve alloy homogeneity and markedly reduce phase segregation relative to a slower-profile control.
